children.prompt: Explain why this shape is a trapezium.

answer.worked: The copied right triangles have $AY\perp AB$ and $BZ\perp AB$. Thus $AY\parallel BZ$, so the outer quadrilateral has a pair of parallel sides and is a trapezium.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Explain why $\angle YXZ$ is a right angle.

answer.worked: Let $\theta=\angle AXY$ and $\phi=\angle BXZ$. The two copied right triangles are congruent, so $\phi=\angle AYX$. The acute angles of triangle $AXY$ give $\theta+\phi=90^\circ$. Since $A,X,B$ are collinear, $\theta+\angle YXZ+\phi=180^\circ$. Therefore $\angle YXZ=90^\circ$. This uses angle sums and congruence, not Pythagoras’ theorem.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Write down the area of the trapezium, in terms of $a$ and $b$, using the formula for the area of a trapezium.

answer.worked: The parallel sides have lengths $a$ and $b$, and their perpendicular separation is $AB=a+b$. Therefore $$A=\frac12(a+b)(a+b)=\frac12(a+b)^2.$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: Find the area of the trapezium, in terms of $a$, $b$ and $c$, by adding up the areas of the three triangles.

answer.worked: The two copied right triangles each have area $\frac12ab$. By part b, the middle triangle is right-angled with perpendicular sides $c$ and $c$, so its area is $\frac12c^2$. Adding gives $$A=\frac12ab+\frac12ab+\frac12c^2=ab+\frac12c^2.$$

answer.short: Both expressions give the area of the same trapezium.

$\begin{aligned}(a+b)^2&=2ab+c^2\\a^2+2ab+b^2&=2ab+c^2\\a^2+b^2&=c^2.\end{aligned}$

answer.short: A round peg in a square hole fits better when “better” means the smaller proportion of unfilled hole area.

The round peg in the square hole wastes the smaller fraction and therefore fits better under these assumptions.

content.prompt: It is now time to make a few observations about your Fibonacci sequences.

children.label: a
children.prompt: The classic sequence (in Activity 1) has two odd seeds. This gives a certain pattern of odd and even terms throughout the sequence. What happens if you start with two even seeds or an odd and an even seed? Explain.

answer.short: Odd/odd seeds: O,O,E repeats. Even/even seeds: every term even. Even/odd seeds: E,O,O repeats; odd/even seeds: O,E,O repeats.
answer.worked: An odd plus an odd is even; an odd plus an even is odd; two evens give an even. Starting with O,O therefore gives O,O,E,O,O,E,... . Starting E,E stays even forever. Starting E,O gives E,O,O,E,O,O,...; reversing the order shifts that three-term pattern. Parity here concerns integer seeds.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Compare the 10th terms in each of the sequences you generated in Activities 2 and 3. Which one is larger? Compare the 20th terms as well. Can you explain what is happening?

answer.short: Sample: $F_{10}$ is $500$ versus $435$; $F_{20}$ is $61495$ versus $53510$. The ascending seed order gives the larger terms from the fourth term onward (equal seeds give identical sequences).
answer.worked: For seeds $6,11$ versus $11,6$, the requested values are $500>435$ and $61495>53510$. More generally compare seeds $a,b$ with $b,a$. Their third terms are both $a+b$. Their fourth terms are $a+2b$ and $2a+b$, a difference $b-a$; the fifth terms again differ by $b-a$. Every later difference is the sum of its two predecessors. Therefore if $b>a$, all differences from the fourth onward are positive. If the seeds are equal the sequences coincide; if $a>b$ the roles reverse.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Use a calculator to divide the term F₁₀ in the first sequence by the term F₉ immediately before it. Write your answer down. Then do the same with the second sequence. Now repeat the calculations but with F₂₀ and F₁₉ for both sequences. Do you notice anything interesting? Did any of the other students who are doing this activity get the same number? Compare how close your ratios are. With positive seeds the later ratios generally get closer; other seed choices can give undefined ratios. Give decimal ratios to six decimal places.

answer.short: Sample ratios: $1.618123$, $1.617100$ at term 10; both $1.618034$ at term 20 (6 d.p.). Positive-seed later ratios approach $\Phi\approx1.618034$; unrestricted seeds may give undefined ratios.
answer.worked: For the sample sequences, $500/309\approx1.618123$ and $435/269\approx1.617100$, whereas $61495/38006\approx1.618034$ and $53510/33071\approx1.618034$ (6d.p.). The earlier values differ already in the third decimal place, so the original sixth-place claim is not valid. For positive seeds repeated addition makes consecutive ratios approach the golden ratio. This is not an unconditional claim for “any” seeds: two zero seeds give $0/0$, and other signed seeds may give a zero denominator or exceptional behaviour.

children.label: d
children.prompt: For the classic Fibonacci sequence, the first two terms larger than 1 000 000 are $F_{31}=1\,346\,269$ and $F_{32}=2\,178\,309$. Use these two values to see if what you noticed in the previous ratio calculations also holds for high-order terms in the classic Fibonacci sequence.

answer.short: $\dfrac{2178309}{1346269}\approx1.618034$ (6d.p.), agreeing with the later sample ratios.
answer.worked: Using the two given values, $2178309/1346269=1.618033988749\ldots$, which rounds to $1.618034$. With the actual source convention $F_1=F_2=1$, these are $F_{31}$ and $F_{32}$; the preceding term is $F_{30}=832040<1000000$, so they are indeed the first two terms above a million. The original indices 32/33 were off by one.

children.label: e
children.prompt:
The number you obtained (to a good approximation) in the ratio calculations is famous and interesting enough to deserve its own Greek letter. It is called Φ (phi, pronounced to rhyme with ‘spy’) and is known as the golden mean or golden ratio. It is a very interesting number with a long history.

Search Google and you will discover some amazing facts about Φ. It appears in many different ways in geometry and architecture.

answer.short: Sample finding: removing a square from a golden rectangle leaves a smaller similar golden rectangle.
answer.worked: This open research instruction has no single required fact. A mathematical sample is the golden rectangle: its longer-to-shorter side ratio is $\Phi$. Removing a square leaves a rectangle with ratio $1/(\Phi-1)=\Phi$, so it is similar to the original.

children.label: f
children.prompt:
Now try calculating these values and see what you notice about them. Give decimal results to six decimal places.

Calculate $\Phi^2$.

answer.worked: Since $\Phi^2=\Phi+1$, division by the positive $\Phi$ gives $\Phi=1+1/\Phi$. Hence $1/\Phi=\Phi-1\approx0.618034$.
Substituting $\Phi=(1+\sqrt5)/2$ gives $2\Phi-1=\sqrt5$, so $(2\Phi-1)^2=5$.

A runaway dog, called Fido, is running at 3 m/s and is being chased by his owner, who is riding her bicycle at 5 m/s. How long will it be before she catches up with the dog?

entries.description: This question is one involving the concept of closing speed. By finding the difference between the front-runner’s speed and the chaser’s speed, the question can be solved very easily. It makes use of the fact that, since speed = distance ÷ time, then it follows that time = distance ÷ speed.

entries.description:
The owner is cycling at (5 − 3) m/s = 2 m/s faster than the dog. This is the speed at which she is closing the distance between herself and Fido. You can imagine that the distance between them is being ‘eaten up’ at the rate of 2 m/s. If you do this, it is obvious that, if Fido is 100 metres ahead when the chase begins, he will be 98 m ahead after 1 second, 96 m ahead after 2 seconds, and after (100 m) ÷ (2 m/s) = 50 s, he will be 0 m ahead. With a 20-m head start, the chase will only last 10 seconds.

We can also use a similar idea to find out where the chase ends. Since the chase lasts for 50 seconds, the owner will travel (50 s) × (5 m/s) = 250 m until she catches the dog. (Fido will have run (50 s) × (3 m/s) = 150 m, which, when added to his 100 m start, will also be 250 m from where his owner started the chase.)
